claims.text: Superconductivity in qualifying high-entropy alloys is governed by the interplay between average valence electron concentration and lattice distortion from atomic-size mismatch.
An optimal valence electron concentration combined with controlled lattice distortion enhances the electron–phonon coupling required for superconductivity.
The proposed starting material is a single-phase solid solution containing at least five elements at concentrations of at least 5 at.% each.
The constituent elements can be selected to provide both substantial atomic-size dispersion and tunable average valence electron concentration.
Elemental substitutions will systematically adjust average valence electron concentration while approximately preserving atomic-size mismatch and a single solid-solution phase.
Using identical processing conditions guarantees that changes in superconducting properties originate from composition.
Atomic-size mismatch induces local lattice distortions.
Local lattice distortions affect phonon spectra and thereby modulate electron–phonon coupling.
Variations in average valence electron concentration alter the electronic density of states at the Fermi level.
Lattice distortion influences phonon softening.
Changes in the density of states and phonon softening jointly modulate electron–phonon interaction strength and determine the superconducting transition temperature.
An optimal balance of valence electron concentration and lattice distortion enhances superconductivity, while deviations reduce the transition temperature or suppress superconductivity.
The superconducting transition temperature will show a dome-shaped dependence on valence electron concentration and lattice distortion.

Alloys near the optimal valence electron concentration with moderate-to-high lattice distortion will have higher transition temperatures than alloys with nonoptimal valence electron concentration or insufficient distortion.
A benchmark Nb-Ta-based or previously characterized titanium-rich high-entropy alloy has known superconducting behavior suitable for use as a baseline.
The hypothesis is restricted to alloys that remain single solid solutions without significant phase segregation or ordering and retain at least five elements at no less than 5 at.% each.
Compositions that destabilize the single phase or introduce secondary phases are outside the hypothesis's domain.
The relative contributions of valence electron concentration and lattice distortion to electron–phonon coupling have not been quantified.
The balance between valence electron concentration and lattice distortion may vary with elemental combination.
The role of local chemical ordering in the proposed alloys is unresolved.
